question: What type of listing agreement is created by Wisconsin's standard WB-1 Residential Listing Contract form?
choice_a: An exclusive right to sell listing, under which the listing firm earns commission regardless of who procures the buyer during the listing term
choice_b: An open listing that lets the seller list the property with multiple firms at the same time
choice_c: An exclusive agency listing that pays no commission if the seller personally finds the buyer
choice_d: A net listing based on a stipulated net price to the owner
explanation: The WRA Forms Library titles WB-1 the "Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell," meaning the firm is entitled to commission no matter who procures the buyer during the term. Net listings like choice D are separately prohibited outright under REEB 24.10.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library (current WB-1 title: "Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell"); net-listing prohibition at Wis. Admin. Code REEB 24.10.

question: Under Wisconsin Administrative Code, why must a listing contract such as the WB-1 be reduced to writing rather than left as an oral agreement between broker and seller?
choice_a: REEB 24.08 requires a licensee to put in writing all listing contracts and other written proposals "expressing the exact agreement of the parties," subject to narrow carve-outs for attorney-drafted writings
choice_b: Wis. Stat. ch. 706 requires every real property listing agreement to be recorded with the county register of deeds
choice_c: Real estate listing contracts are governed by the U.C.C. Statute of Frauds because real estate is treated as a good
choice_d: REEB 15.04 requires oral listing agreements to be reduced to writing only when the transaction price exceeds $100,000
explanation: REEB 24.08 states a licensee shall put in writing all listing contracts, buyer agency agreements, offers to purchase, and other written proposals expressing the exact agreement of the parties, with a carve-out only where the writing is completed by the parties/attorneys or falls outside the licensee's REEB 16 authority.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 16.06, when a licensee reproduces the board-approved WB-11 Residential Offer to Purchase form and the parties do not want a particular optional provision (such as an inspection contingency paragraph) to apply, what must the licensee do?
choice_a: Still show that the optional provision exists on the reproduced form but clearly indicate that it does not apply, rather than silently deleting it
choice_b: Freely delete the optional paragraph from the reproduced form without any indication, since REEB 16.06 governs only mandatory paragraphs
choice_c: Have the deletion notarized before the omission becomes effective
choice_d: Obtain the Real Estate Examining Board's pre-approval each time an optional contingency is left blank
explanation: REEB 16.06 requires reproduced board-approved forms to keep identical numbering, line contents, and page layout and specifically bars omitting optional provisions "without indication" — this is the core rule behind proper contingency drafting.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 16.04, when may a Wisconsin broker use something other than the board-approved WB form to write up a real estate purchase offer?
choice_a: When no board-approved form exists for that type of transaction, or when the parties or their attorneys draft an agreement embodying all of the negotiated terms
choice_b: Whenever the licensee's supervising broker personally approves a substitute form
choice_c: Only when the buyer is paying cash and waives every contingency
choice_d: Never — REEB 16.04 makes use of WB forms mandatory in every transaction without exception
explanation: REEB 16.04 requires licensees to use approved forms except where no approved form exists for the transaction type, or where the parties/attorneys draft an agreement that embodies all the negotiated terms.

question: What is the function of Wisconsin's WB-25 Bill of Sale form in a residential real estate transaction?
choice_a: It documents the transfer of personal property, such as included appliances or furnishings, that is not conveyed by the deed to the real property
choice_b: It transfers title to the real property itself in place of a warranty deed
choice_c: It is the form buyers sign to waive their statutory real estate condition report rights
choice_d: It functions as the lender's closing disclosure summarizing loan charges
explanation: WB-25 is the WRA's standard "Bill of Sale" form, used to convey personal property included in a sale (e.g., appliances, a boat, or business fixtures) separately from the deed that conveys real property.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-25 "Bill of Sale."

question: What relationship does Wisconsin's WB-36 form establish between a real estate firm and a prospective buyer or tenant?
choice_a: A written buyer agency or tenant representation agreement under which the firm acts as agent for the buyer or tenant in the transaction
choice_b: A listing contract giving the firm the exclusive right to sell the buyer's current home
choice_c: A property management agreement between the firm and a landlord
choice_d: A pre-agency showing agreement that creates no agency relationship
explanation: WB-36, "Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement," is the standard form creating an agency relationship in which the firm represents the buyer or tenant, distinct from WB-50 (Residential Pre-agency Showing Agreement), which creates no agency.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-36 "Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement" and WB-50 "Residential Pre-agency Showing Agreement."

question: After a WB-11 Residential Offer to Purchase has been fully accepted by both parties, which Wisconsin standard form is used to change one or more of its terms with the mutual agreement of both parties?
choice_a: WB-40, Amendment to Offer to Purchase
choice_b: WB-44, Counter-Offer
choice_c: WB-46, Multiple Counter-Proposal
choice_d: WB-41, Notice Relating to Offer to Purchase
explanation: WB-40 is used to mutually change the terms of an already-accepted offer. A Counter-Offer (WB-44) and Multiple Counter-Proposal (WB-46) are used before acceptance during negotiation, while a Notice (WB-41) communicates information without changing contract terms.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-40 "Amendment to Offer to Purchase," WB-44 "Counter-Offer," WB-46 "Multiple Counter-Proposal," and WB-41 "Notice Relating to Offer to Purchase."

question: What is the general purpose of Wisconsin's WB-41, Notice Relating to Offer to Purchase, once an offer has been accepted?
choice_a: It provides a standard written format for one party to give the other a notice required or permitted under the accepted offer — for example, that a contingency has or has not been satisfied — without itself changing the contract's terms
choice_b: It cancels the offer to purchase and mutually releases both parties from further obligation
choice_c: It creates a counter-proposal in response to multiple competing offers on the same property
choice_d: It amends the purchase price and closing date stated in the accepted offer
explanation: WB-41 is a general-purpose notice form used to deliver a notice called for under an accepted offer (such as contingency satisfaction/non-satisfaction), distinct from WB-45 (cancellation), WB-46 (multiple counter-proposal), and WB-40 (amendment).
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-41 "Notice Relating to Offer to Purchase."

question: Before a seller has accepted a buyer's WB-11 offer, the seller wants to propose different terms (for example, a higher price) back to the buyer. Which Wisconsin form is designed for this?
choice_a: WB-44, Counter-Offer
choice_b: WB-40, Amendment to Offer to Purchase
choice_c: WB-45, Cancellation Agreement and Mutual Release
choice_d: WB-25, Bill of Sale
explanation: WB-44, Counter-Offer, is used pre-acceptance when one party proposes changed terms back to the other in response to a pending offer.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-44 "Counter-Offer."

question: What does Wisconsin's WB-45, Cancellation Agreement and Mutual Release, accomplish for the parties to an accepted offer to purchase?
choice_a: It documents the parties' mutual agreement to cancel the contract and release each other from further obligations under it, including disposition of earnest money
choice_b: It documents one party's unilateral right to terminate the contract without the other party's consent
choice_c: It transfers the buyer's rights and obligations under the contract to a third-party assignee
choice_d: It extends the closing date without altering any other term of the contract
explanation: WB-45 is the standard form the parties sign together to mutually cancel an accepted offer and release each other from further contractual obligation, including how earnest money will be handled.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-45 "Cancellation Agreement and Mutual Release."

question: A Wisconsin seller has received three competing written offers on the same property and wants to counter more than one of them on identical terms without revealing one buyer's offer terms to another. Which form is intended for this situation, and what related conduct rule constrains how the licensee handles the competing offers?
choice_a: WB-46, Multiple Counter-Proposal; REEB 24.12 prohibits disclosing one prospective buyer's offer terms to a competing buyer
choice_b: WB-40, Amendment to Offer to Purchase; REEB 24.09 prohibits misleading a client about market value
choice_c: WB-41, Notice Relating to Offer to Purchase; REEB 24.10 prohibits net listings
choice_d: WB-44, Counter-Offer; REEB 24.08 requires agreements to be in writing
explanation: WB-46, Multiple Counter-Proposal, lets a seller counter more than one competing offer on the same terms; REEB 24.12(1) separately bars disclosing one prospective buyer's offer terms to a competing buyer or someone who might pass the information along.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-46 "Multiple Counter-Proposal"; Wis. Admin. Code REEB 24.12(1).

question: Under REEB 24.12(2), if a licensee knows that a listed property is subject to another party's right of first refusal, what must the licensee do before sharing a received offer with the holder of that right?
choice_a: Provide written and timely disclosure of the right of first refusal to all interested parties
choice_b: Obtain the Real Estate Examining Board's pre-approval before making any disclosure
choice_c: Wait until closing to disclose the existence of the right of first refusal
choice_d: Nothing further is required, because REEB 24.12(2) applies only to commercial transactions
explanation: REEB 24.12(2) requires written and timely disclosure of a known right of first refusal to all interested parties before the licensee may share an offer with the holder of that right.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1), within how many days after acceptance of a contract of sale or option contract must the seller deliver the real estate condition report to the buyer?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 5 days
choice_c: 15 days
choice_d: 30 days
explanation: Section 709.02(1) requires delivery of the real estate condition report not later than 10 days after acceptance of the contract of sale or option contract.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1), what remedy does a prospective buyer have if the seller fails to deliver the required real estate condition report within the statutory period?
choice_a: The buyer may rescind the contract within 2 business days after the end of the 10-day delivery period and is entitled to return of any deposits or option fees
choice_b: The buyer automatically takes title with no report and no rescission right
choice_c: The buyer must sue for damages equal to triple the purchase price
choice_d: The buyer may only delay closing by an additional 10 days
explanation: Under § 709.02(1), a buyer who does not timely receive the report may rescind within 2 business days after the 10-day period ends, and is entitled to a refund of deposits or option fees paid.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.01(2), which of the following transferors is exempt from the real estate condition report requirement?
choice_a: A personal representative, trustee, conservator, or other court-appointed fiduciary who has never occupied the property being transferred
choice_b: An owner-occupant selling their own home directly to a buyer
choice_c: A licensed real estate broker acting as the seller's listing agent
choice_d: A buyer purchasing the property under a land contract
explanation: Section 709.01(2) exempts fiduciaries such as personal representatives, trustees, and conservators from the condition report requirement, but only if they have never occupied the transferred property.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.135(1), when must a real estate firm give a prospective customer (a party the firm does not represent as agent) the written "Disclosure to Customers" statement?
choice_a: Before the firm negotiates on the customer's behalf in the transaction
choice_b: Only after the transaction has closed, for recordkeeping purposes
choice_c: Only if the customer specifically requests it in writing
choice_d: At the same time the listing contract is signed with the seller-client
explanation: Section 452.135(1) requires firms to provide the written Disclosure to Customers statement before negotiating on the customer's behalf, outlining the duties owed to non-client parties.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.135(2), by what point must a firm furnish a prospective client the written "Disclosure to Clients" statement, and what must the client do as part of that disclosure?
choice_a: By the time an agency agreement is executed; the client must select one of the stated options describing whether and how the same firm may represent both the client and the other party to the transaction
choice_b: Within 10 days after closing; the client must initial each paragraph of the listing contract
choice_c: Before the firm advertises the listed property; the client must choose an asking price
choice_d: At the first showing of the property; the client must sign a lead-based paint acknowledgment
explanation: Section 452.135(2) requires the Disclosure to Clients statement by the time the agency agreement is executed, and requires the client to select among the stated multiple-representation options (with or without designated agency, or no dual representation).

question: A Wisconsin broker is listing a house built in 1965. Under federal lead-based paint disclosure law, which applies in Wisconsin transactions and is implemented through a board-approved disclosure form, what must occur before the buyer becomes obligated under a contract to purchase?
choice_a: The seller must disclose known lead-based paint hazards and provide any available reports, and the buyer must receive the federally required lead hazard information pamphlet, because the home was built before 1978
choice_b: No disclosure is required because the property is a single-family detached home
choice_c: The seller must remediate all lead-based paint in the home before it may be listed
choice_d: Disclosure is required only if the home was built before 1950
explanation: Federal law requires disclosure of known lead-based paint hazards and delivery of the EPA-approved pamphlet before a purchaser becomes obligated under a contract for housing built before 1978; Wisconsin licensees implement this through a board-approved disclosure form used alongside the WB purchase forms.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d; 24 C.F.R. pt. 35 / 40 C.F.R. pt. 745 (federal lead-based paint disclosure applicable to pre-1978 Wisconsin housing transactions, implemented through a board-approved form under Wis. Admin. Code ch. REEB 16).

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 15.02(1), if a licensee transmits a signed offer to purchase to the other side's agent by fax or email, what standard must that transmission meet?
choice_a: It must be an "exact and complete copy" of the document — meaning every page, not merely the signature page — promptly provided to any person who signed it
choice_b: It only needs to include the signature page, since the other pages were already provided in draft form earlier
choice_c: It must be sent by certified mail regardless of any electronic transmission already made
choice_d: It need only be furnished if the receiving party specifically requests it in writing
explanation: REEB 15.02(1) requires a licensee to promptly provide an exact and complete copy of any document used, prepared, or received in real estate practice to anyone who signed it — which means transmitting every page of the contract, not just the page bearing signatures.

question: Under REEB 15.02(2), once an offer to purchase, amendment, or counter-offer has been accepted and signed by all parties, to whom must a licensee promptly distribute an exact and complete copy?
choice_a: The seller, the buyer, the listing broker, and the selling broker
choice_b: Only the party the licensee personally represents
choice_c: Only the closing or title company handling the transaction
choice_d: Only the lender financing the buyer's purchase
explanation: REEB 15.02(2) requires distribution of an accepted/signed offer, amendment, counter-offer, exchange agreement, or option to the seller, buyer, listing broker, and selling broker.

question: Under REEB 15.02(3), when must a broker or salesperson distribute an exact and complete copy of a signed lease or rental agreement to the tenant?
choice_a: Promptly upon execution of the lease or rental agreement
choice_b: Only if the tenant pays an administrative copy fee
choice_c: Within 2 business days after the tenant moves in
choice_d: Only at the landlord's discretion
explanation: REEB 15.02(3) requires prompt distribution of an exact and complete copy of an accepted, signed lease or rental agreement to the tenant upon execution, and to the landlord upon request.

question: Under REEB 15.02(4), when must a broker or salesperson distribute a copy of a signed listing contract or agency agreement to the client?
choice_a: Promptly when the client signs the agency agreement
choice_b: Only when the property actually sells
choice_c: At closing, together with the settlement statement
choice_d: Within 2 years, when the record-retention period begins to run
explanation: REEB 15.02(4) requires prompt distribution of an exact and complete copy of a signed listing contract or agency agreement to the client at the time the client signs it.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 15.04(1), for how long must a firm generally retain exact and complete copies of listing contracts, agency agreements, offers to purchase, leases, closing statements, and trust account records, absent a longer federal requirement or an open investigation?
choice_a: At least 2 years from the date of the transaction or termination of the agency
choice_b: At least 6 years from the date of the transaction
choice_c: At least 1 year from the date of the transaction
choice_d: Indefinitely, with no minimum retention period specified
explanation: REEB 15.04(1) sets a minimum 2-year retention period, running from the transaction date or agency termination, unless a longer federal retention requirement applies or an investigation is pending.

question: Under REEB 15.04(2), what obligation does an individual licensee associated with a firm have regarding transaction documents and records the licensee prepares, uses, or receives?
choice_a: The licensee must submit those documents and records to the firm in a timely manner
choice_b: The licensee may retain the only copy personally for the statutory 2-year period instead of the firm
choice_c: The licensee must destroy personal copies immediately after closing
choice_d: The licensee must file the documents directly with the Real Estate Examining Board
explanation: REEB 15.04(2) requires a licensee associated with a firm to submit transaction-related documents and records to the firm in a timely manner, so the firm can maintain custody consistent with the retention rule.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.132(4)(a), what is a supervising broker generally required to review before a transaction closes?
choice_a: Executed transaction documents, such as agency agreements, offers to purchase, leases, and trust account records associated with the transaction
choice_b: The buyer's personal credit report and tax returns
choice_c: The title insurance commitment exclusively
choice_d: Only documents that a licensee affirmatively flags as problematic
explanation: Section 452.132(4)(a) requires the supervising broker to review executed transaction documents — agency agreements, offers to purchase, leases, trust account records, and related documents — before closing.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.132(4)(b), what is a supervising broker's pre-closing document review limited to confirming?
choice_a: That required disclosure statements were provided and approved forms were used correctly, and communicating apparent errors to the licensee — not certifying the documents' legal sufficiency
choice_b: That the buyer qualifies for financing
choice_c: That the seller's asking price reflects fair market value
choice_d: That the property has passed a home inspection
explanation: Section 452.132(4)(b) limits the review to confirming disclosure statements were furnished and approved forms were properly used, and to communicating apparent errors to the licensee; it does not make the broker a guarantor of legal sufficiency.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.132(5), which type of firm must delegate supervisory responsibility to a licensed individual broker rather than the firm itself acting as its own supervising broker by default?
choice_a: A licensed broker business entity firm
choice_b: A sole proprietorship operated by an individual broker
choice_c: Any firm with fewer than 3 associated licensees
choice_d: A firm that handles only rental property management
explanation: Section 452.132(5) distinguishes licensed broker business entities, which must delegate supervision to a designated individual broker, from other firm structures where the firm itself serves as the supervising broker absent a specific delegation.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.133, how long does a firm's duty to keep a party's confidential information confidential generally last, absent a legal mandate to disclose or the party's authorization?
choice_a: The duty continues even after the transaction is completed
choice_b: The duty ends automatically at closing
choice_c: The duty ends when the listing contract expires, even if the transaction has not closed
choice_d: The duty applies only to information about the firm's own client, never about a customer
explanation: Section 452.133 makes clear that the confidentiality duty persists after the transaction is completed, unless disclosure is legally mandated or specifically authorized by the party the information concerns.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.133, which duty may a client agree in writing to waive, unlike the duties of honesty, reasonable skill and care, disclosure of material adverse facts, and confidentiality, none of which can be waived?
choice_a: The duty to negotiate on the client's behalf
choice_b: The duty to disclose the firm's own compensation arrangement
choice_c: The duty to provide a real estate condition report
choice_d: The duty to use board-approved forms
explanation: Section 452.133 allows a client to waive the negotiation duty under specific written-disclosure conditions, while the duties of honest service, reasonable skill and care, disclosure of material adverse facts, and confidentiality cannot be waived.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(2), which of the following is a licensee NOT required to affirmatively disclose absent a specific buyer inquiry?
choice_a: The location of a licensed adult family home, community-based residential facility, or nursing home in the vicinity of the property
choice_b: A known structural defect in the roof discovered during the licensee's inspection
choice_c: A material inconsistency between the seller's disclosure and a third-party inspection report
choice_d: An undisclosed side agreement affecting the buyer's secured lender
explanation: Section 452.23(2)(c) exempts a licensee from having to disclose the location of adult family homes, community-based residential facilities, or nursing homes; the other listed items are affirmative disclosure duties under REEB 24.07 and § 452.133.

question: Under REEB 24.13(1), may a listing licensee refuse to draft or submit a buyer's written offer to purchase because the licensee personally believes the offered price is too low?
choice_a: No — a licensee may not refuse to draft or submit a written proposal unless its terms are contrary to the other party's specific written instructions
choice_b: Yes — licensees have unrestricted discretion to decline drafting any offer they find personally unfavorable
choice_c: Yes, but only if the buyer is unrepresented by an agent
choice_d: No, unless the offer omits a financing contingency
explanation: REEB 24.13(1) prohibits refusing to draft or submit a written proposal unless the proposed terms are contrary to the other party's specific written instructions — a personal opinion about price is not a valid basis to refuse.

question: Under REEB 24.13(3)(b), when may a licensee associated with the listing firm submit a personal written offer to purchase the listed property while aware of the terms of a pending competing offer?
choice_a: Generally they may not, except that the firm may arrange for a guaranteed sale at the time of listing
choice_b: At any time, as long as the licensee discloses their license status to the seller
choice_c: Only after obtaining the Real Estate Examining Board's written pre-approval
choice_d: Only if the licensee's personal offer is at least 10% above the pending offer
explanation: REEB 24.13(3)(b) bars a licensee associated with the listing firm from submitting a personal offer with knowledge of a pending offer's terms, except where the firm has arranged a guaranteed sale at the time of listing.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.40(2), what is a licensee prohibited from providing regarding a board-approved form such as WB-11, and what may the licensee still provide?
choice_a: The licensee may not give legal advice about a party's rights or a contract's legal effect but may give a general explanation of a form's provisions when completing or delivering it
choice_b: The licensee may never explain any provision of a WB form under any circumstance
choice_c: The licensee may give full legal advice about the form as long as it is provided in writing
choice_d: The licensee may give legal advice only if the licensee also holds an out-of-state attorney license
explanation: Section 452.40(2) bars licensees from giving legal advice about parties' rights, a contract's legal effect, or title, but expressly allows a general explanation of a board-approved form's provisions when completing or delivering the form.

question: Under REEB 16.06, when a firm reproduces a board-approved WB form on its own letterhead, what must it preserve from the original approved form?
choice_a: Identical numbering, line contents, and page layout, along with the board's approval statement and date in the upper left corner
choice_b: Only the general subject matter; the wording may be freely rewritten in plain language
choice_c: Only the signature block; all other content may be customized
choice_d: Nothing — reproduction requirements apply only to State Bar of Wisconsin forms, not WB forms
explanation: REEB 16.06 requires reproduced board-approved forms to retain identical numbering, line contents, and page layout, and to display the board's approval statement and date in the upper left corner, in addition to permitted firm identification.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 24.02(19), which of the following documents falls within the definition of a "written proposal" governed by the drafting-and-submission conduct rules?
choice_a: A notice, offer, counteroffer, option, exchange agreement, rental agreement, or amendment provided by one party to another during a transaction
choice_b: Only a fully executed deed recorded with the register of deeds
choice_c: Only marketing flyers used to advertise a listed property
choice_d: Only documents that have already been reviewed by an attorney
explanation: REEB 24.02(19) defines "written proposal" broadly to include notices, offers, counteroffers, options, exchanges, rental agreements, and amendments exchanged during a transaction — this scope determines which documents REEB 24.13's drafting/submission duties apply to.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 24.10, why is a WB-1 listing contract that pays the firm a stipulated net price to the owner with the firm keeping any excess as commission not permitted in Wisconsin?
choice_a: REEB 24.10 prohibits licensees from obtaining or negotiating any listing contract structured as a net listing to the owner with the excess retained by the firm as commission
choice_b: Such listings are permitted only if disclosed to the buyer in writing before an offer is submitted
choice_c: Such listings are permitted only on commercial property, not residential property
choice_d: REEB 24.10 permits net listings as long as the seller is a licensed attorney
explanation: REEB 24.10 flatly bars net listings, in which the firm's commission is whatever exceeds a stipulated net price to the owner, regardless of disclosure or property type.

question: Under REEB 24.09, when preparing a WB-1 listing contract and advising a prospective seller-client, what is a licensee prohibited from doing?
choice_a: Misleading the potential client about the benefits of using the licensee's services or about the market value of the real estate to be listed
choice_b: Providing any opinion of value at all, even a comparative market analysis
choice_c: Recommending a listing price higher than the seller requests
choice_d: Disclosing the firm's commission rate to the seller before the listing contract is signed
explanation: REEB 24.09 prohibits a licensee from misleading a potential client about the benefits of the licensee's services or about the market value of the property to be listed, leased, or sold — it does not bar giving a value opinion or disclosing commission.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.05(1), if a buyer submits an offer and afterward receives a real estate condition report disclosing a defect, what right does the buyer have regarding that contract?
choice_a: The buyer may rescind the contract in writing, before the applicable deadline, based on the disclosed defect without liability, and is entitled to return of any deposits or option fees paid
choice_b: The buyer must proceed to closing regardless of any defect first disclosed after the offer is submitted
choice_c: The buyer may only renegotiate the purchase price, not rescind, once an offer has already been submitted
choice_d: The buyer may rescind only if the defect involves the structural foundation of the home
explanation: Section 709.05(1) gives a buyer who receives a condition report disclosing a defect after submitting the contract the right to rescind in writing before the applicable deadline, without liability, and to recover any deposits or option fees paid.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.05(2)(a)1., can a buyer rescind a contract based on a defect that was already disclosed in a complete real estate condition report the buyer received BEFORE submitting the contract of sale?
choice_a: No — a buyer who received a complete report before submitting the contract may not rescind on the basis of a defect disclosed in that report
choice_b: Yes, the buyer retains an unconditional right to rescind for any disclosed defect regardless of when the report was received
choice_c: Yes, but only if the buyer rescinds within 30 days after closing
choice_d: No, unless the disclosed defect relates to the roof or foundation specifically
explanation: Section 709.05(2)(a)1. bars rescission based on a defect that was already disclosed in a complete report the buyer received before submitting the contract of sale or option contract.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.05(2)(b), when is a buyer barred from rescinding a contract based on a defect disclosed in a real estate condition report?
choice_a: When the buyer was aware of the defect, or was given written notice of it, at or before the time the buyer submitted the contract
choice_b: Only after the buyer has already taken occupancy of the property
choice_c: Whenever the seller happens to be a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Only when the defect resulted from ordinary wear and tear
explanation: Section 709.05(2)(b) precludes rescission for a defect the buyer was already aware of, or had received written notice of, at or before submitting the contract — the disclosure adds nothing new for that buyer.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.05(4), what does the statute establish about the relationship between the right to rescind and other potential remedies available under chapter 709?
choice_a: The right to rescind under s. 709.05 is the only remedy available under chapter 709
choice_b: A buyer may elect either rescission or specific performance as alternative remedies under chapter 709
choice_c: Chapter 709 additionally authorizes a buyer to recover punitive damages on top of rescission
choice_d: The seller, not the buyer, controls whether rescission or a damages remedy applies under chapter 709
explanation: Section 709.05(4) states plainly that the right to rescind under that section is the only remedy under chapter 709, meaning the condition-report statute itself does not create a separate damages remedy.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.035, if a seller obtains new information after completing the real estate condition report but before the contract is accepted, and that information would change one of the report's responses, what must the resulting amendment include?
choice_a: The property's address, the owner's name, the date of the report being amended, the number of the affected statement, and how the original response changed (with an explanation if the response is changed to "yes")
choice_b: Only the seller's updated signature and the anticipated closing date
choice_c: A brand-new inspection report prepared by a licensed engineer
choice_d: Nothing specific — amendments to a condition report have no required content under Wisconsin law
explanation: Section 709.035 lists the required contents of an amendment: the property address, owner's name, date of the original report, the number of the statement affected, how the response changed, and — if changed to "yes" — an explanation why.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.07, when is an owner NOT liable for an error or omission in a real estate condition report?
choice_a: When the owner had no knowledge of the error or omission and it was based on information from a public agency, a licensed engineer, a professional land surveyor, a structural pest control operator, a qualified third party, or a contractor regarding matters within the contractor's occupation
choice_b: Owners are strictly liable for every error or omission in a condition report no matter the source of the information
choice_c: Only if the report was prepared entirely by the listing broker rather than the owner
choice_d: Only if the buyer had already waived the right to receive the report
explanation: Section 709.07 precludes owner liability for an error or omission where the owner had no knowledge of it and it rested on information from a public agency, licensed engineer, professional land surveyor, structural pest control operator, qualified third party, or contractor within the scope of the contractor's occupation.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.08, may a prospective buyer agree in writing to waive the seller's obligation to furnish a real estate condition report altogether?
choice_a: Yes — a buyer may waive in writing the right to receive the report required under s. 709.02
choice_b: No — furnishing a real estate condition report is a non-waivable duty in every transfer subject to chapter 709
choice_c: Only a circuit court order can authorize waiving the report requirement
choice_d: A buyer may waive receipt of the report only in condominium-unit transactions
explanation: Section 709.08 expressly permits a buyer to waive in writing the right to receive the report required under s. 709.02, contrary to the common misconception that the condition report can never be waived.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.08, what happens to a buyer's right to rescind under § 709.05 once the buyer proceeds to closing?
choice_a: The right to rescind is terminated once the buyer proceeds to closing
choice_b: The right to rescind survives closing and remains exercisable for 2 years afterward
choice_c: Closing has no effect at all on the right to rescind under chapter 709
choice_d: The right to rescind automatically converts into a damages claim at closing
explanation: Section 709.08 provides that if a buyer proceeds to closing, the buyer's right to rescind under s. 709.05 is terminated.

question: Wisconsin's separate "vacant land disclosure report" under Wis. Stat. § 709.033 is the required disclosure form for which category of real property, as defined in § 709.001(5)(b)?
choice_a: Real property containing no buildings
choice_b: Previously occupied real property with 1 to 4 dwelling units
choice_c: Commercial property with more than 4 rental units
choice_d: Newly constructed, never-occupied single-family homes
explanation: Section 709.033 supplies the required disclosure report form for real property defined in § 709.001(5)(b) — property containing no buildings — as a distinct form from the residential condition report used for 1-4 unit dwellings under § 709.03.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.001(5)(a), the real estate condition report requirement covers real property with 1 to 4 dwelling units EXCEPT for which category?
choice_a: Property that has never been inhabited, such as new construction that has not yet been occupied
choice_b: Property that happens to be owner-occupied at the time it is listed
choice_c: Property being sold through a licensed real estate broker rather than for sale by owner
choice_d: Property located within an incorporated city rather than a township
explanation: Section 709.001(5)(a) defines "real property" for condition-report purposes as 1-4 dwelling-unit property, expressly excluding property that has never been inhabited — which is why never-occupied new construction is generally outside the condition-report requirement.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.02(2), when a transfer involves a condominium unit, what must the owner additionally furnish as an addendum to the real estate condition report?
choice_a: The condominium's name and creation date, the unit number, seller contact information, the association's name, address, management status and representative contact information, the amount and payment status of current assessments and fees, and a copy of the executive summary required under s. 703.33(1)(h) unless excused
choice_b: A separate condition report about the unit completed and signed by the condominium association's board president
choice_c: Copies of every other unit owner's individual condition report in the same building
choice_d: Proof that the association carries at least $1 million in general liability insurance coverage
explanation: Section 709.02(2) requires condominium-specific addendum disclosures covering the condominium's identifying information, association details, current assessment amounts and payment status, and the executive summary required under s. 703.33(1)(h) unless excused.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.03, how is a "defect" defined for purposes of the residential real estate condition report?
choice_a: A condition that would have a significant adverse effect on the property's value, would significantly impair the health or safety of future occupants, or, if not repaired, removed, or replaced, would significantly shorten or adversely affect the premises' expected normal life
choice_b: Any condition a buyer's home inspector notes on an inspection report, regardless of severity
choice_c: Any condition that would cost more than $500 to correct
choice_d: Any condition that violates the applicable municipal building code, regardless of its effect on value or safety
explanation: Section 709.03's form defines "defect" using the three-prong test: significant adverse effect on value, significant impairment of future occupants' health or safety, or significant shortening/adverse effect on the premises' expected normal life if left unrepaired.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 16.03(1)(a), which category of approved forms — distinct from the WB forms prepared by the Real Estate Examining Board — covers deeds, mortgages, mortgage notes, and land contracts?
choice_a: Forms prepared and approved by the State Bar of Wisconsin
choice_b: Forms drafted ad hoc by whichever party's personal attorney is involved in the transaction
choice_c: Forms published exclusively by the Wisconsin REALTORS Association
choice_d: Forms prepared by the county register of deeds office
explanation: REEB 16.03(1)(a) approves State Bar of Wisconsin forms for deeds, mortgages, mortgage notes, truth-in-lending disclosures, land contracts, releases and satisfactions of mortgage, and assignments of mortgage or land contract — separate from the board's own WB forms.

question: Under Wis. Admin. Code REEB 16.07, what is the stated consequence of a licensee violating any provision of REEB chapter 16 governing approved forms?
choice_a: The violation demonstrates incompetency to act as a real estate licensee for purposes of s. 452.14(3)(i), Stats., and constitutes a violation of s. 452.14(3)(m), Stats.
choice_b: No formal consequence attaches because REEB 16 is advisory guidance rather than a binding administrative rule
choice_c: The violation results only in an informal warning letter with no disciplinary record
choice_d: The violation automatically voids the underlying real estate transaction
explanation: REEB 16.07 ties a violation of chapter REEB 16 directly to the statutory disciplinary grounds in s. 452.14(3)(i) (incompetency) and s. 452.14(3)(m), Stats.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.135(1)(b), if a firm provides brokerage services as a subagent of a principal firm, what disclosure obligation does the subagent firm have?
choice_a: The subagent must provide the Disclosure to Customers statement to any person receiving brokerage services who is not the principal firm's client
choice_b: The subagent has no independent disclosure obligation, since only the principal firm must disclose to customers
choice_c: The subagent must disclose only the commission split it has arranged with the principal firm
choice_d: The subagent must obtain the principal firm's written pre-approval before contacting any customer
explanation: Section 452.135(1)(b) requires a subagent providing brokerage services to a principal firm's customer to independently furnish the Disclosure to Customers statement to that person.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.135(2)(b), for residential property with 1 to 4 dwelling units, if the Disclosure to Clients statement is not incorporated directly into the agency agreement, what must the firm do?
choice_a: Request the client's signed acknowledgment of receipt of the disclosure statement
choice_b: Record the disclosure statement with the county register of deeds
choice_c: Provide the disclosure orally only, since a signature is not required in that circumstance
choice_d: Wait until closing to obtain any acknowledgment that the disclosure was made
explanation: Section 452.135(2)(b) requires a firm to request the client's signed acknowledgment of receipt when the Disclosure to Clients statement for 1-4 unit residential property is not built into the agency agreement itself.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(2)(a), a licensee is not required to disclose that a property was the site of a specific act or occurrence (such as a death or a felony) under what condition?
choice_a: If the act or occurrence had no effect on the physical condition of the property
choice_b: Under no condition — such facts must always be disclosed if the licensee knows them
choice_c: Only if the act or occurrence took place more than 50 years before the listing
choice_d: Only if the buyer is represented through a subagency relationship
explanation: Section 452.23(2)(a) excuses a licensee from disclosing that a property was the site of a specific act or occurrence — the classic "stigmatized property" exemption — as long as that act or occurrence had no effect on the property's physical condition.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(2)(b) and (3), if a qualified third party's written report already discloses certain information about the property, but the licensee independently knows facts that contradict that report, what must the licensee do?
choice_a: Disclose the facts known to the licensee that contradict the third-party report, even though relying on such a report would otherwise excuse further disclosure of that information
choice_b: Nothing further — reliance on a qualified third-party report always fully excuses any additional disclosure duty
choice_c: Discard the third-party report so that it does not conflict with the licensee's own knowledge
choice_d: Disclose the contradiction only if the buyer specifically asks about that exact topic
explanation: While § 452.23(2)(b) excuses disclosure of information already covered by a qualified third party's written report, § 452.23(3) requires the licensee to disclose facts the licensee actually knows that contradict that report.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(2)(d), a licensee is not required to disclose information about sex offender registration requirements except as provided under which statute?
choice_a: Wis. Stat. § 452.24
choice_b: Wis. Stat. § 709.02
choice_c: Wis. Stat. § 706.02
choice_d: Wis. Stat. § 452.14
explanation: Section 452.23(2)(d) exempts a licensee from disclosing sex offender registration information except to the extent § 452.24 separately requires it.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(4), what standard governs a licensee's inspections of property and the disclosures the licensee makes as a result?
choice_a: The degree of care that a reasonably prudent licensee would exercise
choice_b: A strict-liability standard under which any inaccuracy is automatically a violation
choice_c: No standard of care applies, because licensees have no duty to inspect property at all
choice_d: The same expert technical standard of care required of a licensed home inspector
explanation: Section 452.23(4) holds licensees to the degree of care that a reasonably prudent licensee would exercise in inspecting property and making resulting disclosures — not a strict-liability or expert-inspector standard.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 452.23(5), if a licensee makes a disclosure in good-faith reliance on information from a governmental agency, when does the licensee remain exposed to liability for that disclosure?
choice_a: Only if the licensee actually knew the governmental information was inaccurate
choice_b: The licensee is always fully protected from liability no matter what the licensee actually knew
choice_c: The licensee is liable whenever the governmental information later turns out to be wrong, regardless of the licensee's own knowledge
choice_d: The protection applies only to disclosures about zoning classifications, never environmental conditions
explanation: Section 452.23(5) shields a licensee who relies in good faith on governmental information unless the licensee knew that information was inaccurate — actual knowledge of the inaccuracy defeats the protection.

question: Which Wisconsin form would a listing firm use to obtain an exclusive right to sell listing on a client's working farm, as distinct from WB-1?
choice_a: WB-2, Farm Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell
choice_b: WB-1, Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell
choice_c: WB-5, Commercial Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell
choice_d: WB-24, Option to Purchase
explanation: The WRA Forms Library lists WB-2 as the "Farm Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell," structured the same as WB-1 but for farm property listings.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-2 "Farm Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell" (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: A firm is asked to list a vacant residential lot for sale and, separately, a condominium unit for sale. Which Wisconsin forms are the corresponding exclusive right to sell listing contracts?
choice_a: WB-3, Vacant Land Listing Contract, for the lot, and WB-4, Residential Condominium Listing Contract, for the unit
choice_b: WB-1 for both, since WB-1 covers all residential property types
choice_c: WB-4 for the lot and WB-3 for the unit
choice_d: WB-24 for both, since the listing and option forms are interchangeable
explanation: The WRA Forms Library distinguishes WB-3 "Vacant Land Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell" for unimproved land from WB-4 "Residential Condominium Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell" for condominium units.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-3 and WB-4 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: What distinguishes Wisconsin's WB-5 Commercial Listing Contract from its WB-6 Business Listing Contract?
choice_a: WB-5 lists commercial real property for sale, while WB-6 lists the sale of a business enterprise, which may or may not include real estate
choice_b: WB-5 and WB-6 are identical forms differing only in the listing firm's letterhead
choice_c: WB-6 is used only for listing residential rental property
choice_d: WB-5 is used exclusively for auction sales, while WB-6 covers private negotiated sales
explanation: WB-5, "Commercial Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell," lists commercial real property, while WB-6, "Business Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell," lists the sale of a business enterprise — paralleling the WB-16/WB-17 business offer-to-purchase distinction.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-5 and WB-6 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: A buyer wants to submit an offer to purchase a working dairy farm rather than a single-family residence. Which Wisconsin board-approved offer form is designed for that transaction?
choice_a: WB-12, Farm Offer to Purchase
choice_b: WB-11, Residential Offer to Purchase
choice_c: WB-13, Vacant Land Offer to Purchase
choice_d: WB-2, Farm Listing Contract
explanation: WB-12, "Farm Offer to Purchase," is the board-approved offer form for farm property, distinct from WB-11 (residential) and from WB-2 (the listing contract the seller's firm uses, not the buyer's offer).
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-12 "Farm Offer to Purchase" (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: A buyer submits an offer to purchase an unimproved residential lot using Wisconsin's WB-13 form. Under Wis. Stat. § 709.033, what disclosure report must the seller furnish in that transaction, since the property contains no buildings?
choice_a: The vacant land disclosure report set out in § 709.033, rather than the residential real estate condition report used for 1-4 unit dwellings
choice_b: No disclosure report of any kind, because vacant land is entirely exempt from chapter 709
choice_c: The same residential real estate condition report required under § 709.03
choice_d: A federal lead-based paint disclosure, regardless of whether any structure exists on the land
explanation: WB-13, "Vacant Land Offer to Purchase," is used for property containing no buildings as defined in § 709.001(5)(b); such property triggers the distinct vacant land disclosure report under § 709.033, not the residential condition report.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-13 "Vacant Land Offer to Purchase"; Wis. Stat. §§ 709.033, 709.001(5)(b).

question: A buyer uses Wisconsin's WB-14 form to offer to purchase a condominium unit. Under Wis. Stat. § 709.02(2), what must accompany the standard real estate condition report in that transaction?
choice_a: A condominium addendum disclosing the condominium's identifying information, association details, current assessments, and the executive summary required under § 703.33(1)(h) unless excused
choice_b: Nothing additional, since condominium units are entirely exempt from the real estate condition report requirement
choice_c: A separate report completed by the condominium association's board president in place of the owner's report
choice_d: A federal lead-based paint disclosure regardless of the building's age
explanation: WB-14, "Residential Condominium Offer to Purchase," is used for condominium-unit sales, which under § 709.02(2) require a condominium-specific addendum in addition to the base condition report.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-14 "Residential Condominium Offer to Purchase"; Wis. Stat. § 709.02(2).

question: A buyer drafts an offer on Wisconsin's WB-15 Commercial Offer to Purchase form to buy an office building. Why does this transaction NOT trigger the real estate condition report requirement of Wis. Stat. § 709.03?
choice_a: Because chapter 709's disclosure requirements reach only property with 1 to 4 dwelling units and vacant land, not commercial property
choice_b: Because commercial buyers are conclusively presumed to have waived the report under § 709.08
choice_c: Because the report requirement applies only when the buyer is represented by the listing firm
choice_d: Because REEB 16.04 exempts all commercial transactions from using any board-approved form
explanation: WB-15 is used for commercial real property, which falls outside the definition of "real property" for condition-report purposes under § 709.001(5), which reaches only 1-4 dwelling-unit residential property and vacant land.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-15 "Commercial Offer to Purchase"; Wis. Stat. § 709.001(5).

question: What is the key difference between Wisconsin's WB-16 and WB-17 offer to purchase forms when a buyer is purchasing an existing business?
choice_a: WB-16, Offer to Purchase — Business With Real Estate, is used when the sale includes the underlying real property, while WB-17, Offer to Purchase — Business Without Real Estate, is used when only the business itself is being sold
choice_b: WB-16 is used for franchises, while WB-17 is used for sole proprietorships
choice_c: WB-16 is used when the buyer pays cash, while WB-17 is used when the buyer obtains seller financing
choice_d: WB-16 and WB-17 are duplicate forms retained only for historical numbering reasons
explanation: The WRA Forms Library distinguishes WB-16 "Offer to Purchase — Business With Real Estate" from WB-17 "Offer to Purchase — Business Without Real Estate" based on whether real property is included in the business sale.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-16 and WB-17 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: How does Wisconsin's WB-24 Option to Purchase differ from a bilateral offer to purchase such as WB-11, and why does Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1) treat an accepted option contract the same as an accepted contract of sale?
choice_a: An option gives the optionee the right, but not the obligation, to purchase within a stated period in exchange for option consideration, and § 709.02(1) starts the same 10-day condition-report clock running upon acceptance of either an option contract or a contract of sale
choice_b: An option is a unilateral gift requiring no consideration, so it never triggers any condition-report obligation
choice_c: An option and a bilateral offer are legally identical, differing only in form number
choice_d: An option obligates the optionee to close within 10 days, unlike a bilateral offer to purchase
explanation: WB-24, "Option to Purchase," grants the optionee an exclusive right (not a duty) to purchase during the option period; because § 709.02(1) expressly starts its 10-day report-delivery clock upon "acceptance of a contract of sale or option contract," an accepted option is treated the same as an accepted purchase contract for that purpose.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-24 "Option to Purchase"; Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1).

question: What distinguishes Wisconsin's WB-26 Timeshare Contract from its WB-27 Time Share Contract?
choice_a: WB-26 is used for the sale of a timeshare interest by the developer, while WB-27 is used for the resale of a timeshare interest by an owner who is not the developer
choice_b: WB-26 applies to weekly timeshares, while WB-27 applies to fractional quarterly timeshares
choice_c: WB-26 and WB-27 are the same form republished under a new number after a forms revision
choice_d: WB-27 is used only for timeshare property located outside Wisconsin
explanation: The WRA Forms Library titles WB-26 "Timeshare Contract (Sale by Developer)" and WB-27 "Time Share Contract (Resale by Non-Developer)," distinguishing an original developer sale from a subsequent resale.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-26 and WB-27 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: What is the general purpose of Wisconsin's WB-28 Cooperative Agreement and WB-29 Commercial Cooperative Agreement between two real estate firms?
choice_a: They establish the terms of cooperation and compensation between a listing firm and another firm that procures a buyer or tenant for the listed property, with WB-29 serving as the commercial-transaction counterpart to WB-28
choice_b: They create an agency relationship directly between the seller and the cooperating firm's buyer-client
choice_c: They are used exclusively to disclose commission splits to unlicensed referral sources
choice_d: They substitute for a listing contract when no listing contract has been signed
explanation: WB-28, "Cooperative Agreement," and WB-29, "Commercial Cooperative Agreement," are the WRA's standard forms establishing cooperation and compensation terms between a listing firm and a cooperating firm, mirrored across residential and commercial practice.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-28 and WB-29 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: A firm is engaged to find a tenant for a client's rental property rather than to sell it. Which Wisconsin listing form is designed for that engagement?
choice_a: WB-37, Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Rent
choice_b: WB-1, Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Sell
choice_c: WB-36, Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement
choice_d: WB-50, Residential Pre-agency Showing Agreement
explanation: WB-37, "Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Rent," is the landlord-side listing form for renting out residential property, distinct from WB-1's sale listing and from WB-36, which represents a tenant rather than a landlord.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-37 "Residential Listing Contract — Exclusive Right to Rent" (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: How do Wisconsin's WB-38 and WB-39 forms relate to WB-36, Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement?
choice_a: WB-38, Commercial Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement, is the commercial-transaction counterpart to WB-36, while WB-39, Tenant Representation Agreement, represents a tenant specifically rather than establishing broader buyer agency
choice_b: WB-38 and WB-39 replaced WB-36, which is no longer a board-approved form
choice_c: WB-38 is used only for out-of-state buyers, and WB-39 only for cash buyers
choice_d: WB-38 and WB-39 apply exclusively to listing contracts, not to agency agreements with buyers or tenants
explanation: The WRA Forms Library lists WB-38, "Commercial Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement," and WB-39, "Tenant Representation Agreement," alongside WB-36, reflecting parallel agency forms tailored to commercial transactions and tenant-only representation, respectively.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-36, WB-38, and WB-39 titles (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: After a seller has signed a WB-1 listing contract with a firm, the seller and firm want to mutually extend the listing period. Which Wisconsin form is designed for that purpose?
choice_a: WB-42, Amendment to Listing
choice_b: WB-40, Amendment to Offer to Purchase
choice_c: WB-45, Cancellation Agreement and Mutual Release
choice_d: WB-47, Amendment to Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement
explanation: WB-42, "Amendment to Listing," is the counterpart to WB-40 used to modify the terms of an already-signed listing contract (such as WB-1 through WB-6 or WB-37), rather than an offer to purchase.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-42 "Amendment to Listing" (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: A buyer and firm who previously signed a WB-36 Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement want to mutually change one of its terms, such as extending its term. Which Wisconsin form accomplishes this?
choice_a: WB-47, Amendment to Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement
choice_b: WB-42, Amendment to Listing
choice_c: WB-46, Multiple Counter-Proposal
choice_d: WB-44, Counter-Offer
explanation: WB-47, "Amendment to Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement," mutually modifies the terms of an already-signed WB-36, WB-38, or WB-39 agency agreement, paralleling WB-42's role for listing contracts and WB-40's role for offers to purchase.
source_note: WRA Wisconsin Real Estate Forms Library, current WB-47 "Amendment to Buyer Agency/Tenant Representation Agreement" (Products/Forms/Library/Forms_Library_List).

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.04, where must an owner indicate compliance with chapter 709's disclosure requirements?
choice_a: On the contract of sale or option contract, on the closing statement, or in an addendum to one of those documents
choice_b: Only in a standalone affidavit recorded with the county register of deeds
choice_c: Only orally, communicated to the buyer's agent at closing
choice_d: Compliance need not be indicated anywhere; delivering the report itself is legally sufficient with no further indication
explanation: Section 709.04 requires the owner to indicate compliance with chapter 709 on the contract of sale or option contract, on the closing statement, or in an addendum to one of those documents.

question: Under Wis. Stat. § 709.06, what standard governs an owner's performance of the acts and disclosures required by chapter 709?
choice_a: The owner must perform each required act and make each required disclosure with honesty in fact
choice_b: The owner is held to a strict-liability standard regardless of honesty or knowledge
choice_c: The owner need only substantially comply, judged by an objective reasonable-person standard
choice_d: The owner's good faith is conclusively presumed and may never be challenged by a buyer
explanation: Section 709.06 establishes a "good faith" standard requiring the owner to perform each act and make each disclosure required by chapter 709 with honesty in fact.
